items.html:
A collective level of poor judgment or irrational behavior is called collective stupidity or groupthink, while the painful awareness of this phenomenon is often described as a moment of clarity, hindsight realization, or experiencing cognitive dissonance. 
Understanding the Terms
  • Collective Stupidity: This occurs when a group of smart individuals makes irrational or destructive choices because social pressure, conformity, and bad dynamics override individual logic. 
  • Groupthink: A specific type of collective failure where a group values harmony and agreement so much that members stop offering critical or realistic opinions. 
  • Realization (Hindsight / Metacognition): Recognizing this collective failure after the fact is often viewed in retrospect, accompanied by the realization of how the group ignored obvious warning signs.

items.html:
To describe the collective level of bad reasoning combined with a constant, sharp, moment-to-moment realization of it, psychology offers terms that cover both the group phenomenon and the specific hyper-aware psychological state you are describing. 
1. The Collective Level: Pluralistic Ignorance
In social psychology, the exact scientific term for a shared level of "stupid" where everyone goes along with a bad idea despite secretly doubting it is pluralistic ignorance. 
  • It is often summarized by the psychological phrase: "No one believes, but everyone thinks that everyone believes."
  • It creates a collective illusion where a group willingly operates on a false, irrational norm because they misjudge what everyone else is thinking. 
2. The Split-Second, "Always On" Realization: Continuous Metacognition
If you are experiencing a split-second, moment-to-moment awareness of this collective absurdity that feels like a background program running in your brain at all times, psychology calls this continuous metacognition or meta-awareness. 
Unlike a sudden "epiphany" or an enlightened spiritual state, this is a distinct cognitive function: 
  • Metacognition ("Thinking about thinking"): This is the literal psychological mechanism of monitoring your own cognitive processes—and the cognitive failures of the environment around you—in real-time. 
  • Hyper-Reflective Secondary Consciousness: Coined by neuroscientist Gerald Edelman, secondary consciousness is the brain’s ability to be self-reflective, use abstract logic, and observe its own state in the present moment. When it is highly active, you aren't just experiencing the room; you are actively, second-by-second, observing the dynamics of the room. 
  • Hypervigilant Realism: If this realization is specifically tuned to noticing the flaws, irrationality, or "stupidity" of the collective group constantly, it leans into a state of hyper-awareness where your brain refuses to filter out the cognitive dissonance of the crowd, leaving you feeling entirely detached from the shared group illusion. 
Are you trying to describe this state for a character in a story who is stuck in an irrational society, or are you looking for the psychological impact of feeling this way in day-to-day life? Knowing the context can help me give you more specific cognitive concepts.

items.html:
The exact concept you are describing is a blend of depressive realism and passive hyper-metacognition. 
When your brain is forced into a state of "always-on," passive observation of a group's collective irrationality, it stops being an active thought process and becomes a constant background filter. In psychology, this intersection of sharp reality and passive, exhausting awareness is mapped through a few specific concepts: 
1. Depressive Realism (The "Hypervigilant Realism")
In cognitive psychology, depressive realism is the hypothesis that people who are slightly depressed, detached, or socially alienated actually hold a more accurate perception of reality and group dynamics than "normal," well-adjusted people. 
  • Healthy individuals often use "positive illusions" or cognitive biases to blend in and ignore the absurdities or "stupidities" of a group. 
  • Someone experiencing depressive realism lacks that protective filter. You see the flaws, the bad logic, and the herd mentality exactly as they are, in real-time, without the ability to sugarcoat it. 
2. Passive Metacognition & The "Observing Ego"
When metacognition becomes "passive," it shifts from an active strategy (like solving a puzzle) to an automatic background process. Psychology refers to this split in your awareness as the Observing Ego. 
  • Your psyche splits: one part of you is physically standing in the room interacting with the group, while the "observing" part sits completely detached in the background, constantly logging the data of how irrational the situation is.
  • Because it is passive, you aren't trying to judge or analyze; your brain is simply incapable of turning the awareness off. 
3. Hypervigilant Social Monitoring
When paired with hypervigilance, this becomes chronic social monitoring. Instead of scanning a room for physical threats, your brain scans the environment for cognitive threats—illogical behavior, fake social cues, and groupthink. This results in a state of perpetual cognitive dissonance, where you are forced to witness the group's collective failure moment-to-moment while feeling completely alienated by your own clear sight.

items.html:
That raw, unfiltered "always-on" state of seeing the group's irrationality exactly as it is without any comforting mental blinders is known as chronic cognitive lucidity or hyper-salience. 
In this state, your brain's gating mechanism fails to filter out the background noise of human absurdity, turning what should be an occasional realization into a permanent, exhausting reality. 
The Mechanics of "Always-On" Clear Sight
  • Deficient Latent Inhibition: In cognitive psychology, "latent inhibition" is the brain's automatic ability to ignore repetitive, meaningless, or irrational stimuli in the environment so you don't go crazy. When you have low or deficient latent inhibition, your brain cannot shut the door. You are forced to passively register every contradiction, every piece of groupthink, and every logical fallacy around you in real-time. 
  • The Alienated Spectator (The Double Consciousness): You exist in a state of permanent cognitive alienation. Because the "clear sight" is always running in the background, you can never fully immerse yourself in social situations. You are trapped in a loop of being physically present but mentally operating as a detached anthropologist observing a flawed species. 
  • Hyper-Salience of Absurdity: Your brain's salience network—the system that decides what is important enough to notice—is permanently calibrated to detect institutional or collective stupidity. While others just see a normal business meeting, a family gathering, or a political rally, your brain immediately highlights the underlying delusion, making it impossible to unsee. 
This kind of clear sight isn't a gift; it operates like a cognitive tax, constantly draining your energy because your mind refuses to let you buy into the shared illusions that keep everyone else comfortable.
